title: Future forms: Will, be going to, present continuous

explanation.markdown:
## Future forms: Grammar chart

![Future forms – will, be going to, present continuous](/uploads/grammar/b1/future-forms/img-1.png)

## Predictions

We use [**will**](https://test-english.com/grammar-points/a1/will-and-shall/) to talk about something we **think** that will happen:

-   *I think he’**ll win** the election.*
-   *He **will be** a good doctor.*

We use [**be going to**](https://test-english.com/grammar-points/a1/be-going-to-plans-predictions/) to talk about something that is very near to happen or that we **see** is going to happen (there is present evidence)

-   *Don’t drive like a crazy man. We’**re going to have** an accident!*
-   *The doctor said I’**m going to have** a girl.*

## Decisions

We use **will** for decisions that we take at the moment of speaking (**instant decisions)**.

-   ‘*Oh, we don’t have sugar.’ ‘Don’t worry, I’**ll buy** some.’*

We use **be going to** for decisions that we have already taken at the moment of speaking (**intentions or plans**).

-   *‘Why are you undressing?’ ‘Because I’**m going** to go to the swimming pool.’*

## Arrangements

We often use the [**present continuous**](https://test-english.com/grammar-points/a1/present-continuous/) to talk about future events that have already been planned or decided. When we use the **present continuous** for arrangements, we must always include **when** (*at* *7,* *this evening, next month*, etc.) in the sentence.

-   *I’**m seeing** the dentist at 6.*
-   *We **are getting** married next week.*
-   *I’**m flying** to New York tomorrow morning.*

We can also use **be going to** for future arrangements.

-   *I’**m going to** play tennis with Elisabeth today.* 

## Future time clauses (**when**, **as soon as**, **until**, **before**, **after**)

Use the **present simple** to talk about the future in [future time clauses](https://test-english.com/grammar-points/a2/first-conditional-future-time-clauses/) with **when, as soon as, until, before** and **after**.

-   *I’ll retire when I**‘ll be** 70. ![](/uploads/grammar/b1/future-forms/img-2.png)* 
-   *I’ll retire when I**‘m** 70. ![](/uploads/grammar/b1/future-forms/img-3.png)* 
-   *I won’t call you until I **will arrive**. ![](/uploads/grammar/b1/future-forms/img-4.png)* 
-   *I won’t call you until I **arrive***. *![](/uploads/grammar/b1/future-forms/img-5.png)*

## Other uses of **will**

#### Promises and refusals

-   *I **will help** you whenever you need me.*   
-   *I **won’t lend** him my car.* 

#### Future facts

-   *The president **will visit** the Vatican next November.*

#### Offers

We use **I will** in statements or **shall** **I** in questions.

-   *I’**ll carry** that bag for you.*
-   ***Shall*** *I **organise** the meeting?*

#### Suggestions

We use **shall we…?**

-   ***Shall*** *we **eat** out today?*

#### Requests

When we ask someone to do something for us.

-   ***Will*** *you **open** the door, please?*

## **May** or **might** as a future form

We use **may** or **might** for possible actions in the future (when ‘we are not sure’). Compare:

-   *I’**ll be** late for dinner today.* (=I am sure.)
-   *I **might** **be** late for dinner today.* (=It’s possible, but I am not sure.)
-   *I’**m going** to Denmark next September*. (=Sure.)
-   *I **might go** to Denmark next September.* (=Not sure.)

We use [**may** or **might**](https://test-english.com/grammar-points/a2/may-and-might-whats-the-difference/) for things that will possibly happen in the future, but we are not too sure. It’s like a prediction about something that we think perhaps will happen.

-   *The economy **might suffer** a global recession next year.*
-   *Temperatures **may go up** next week.*

We use **may** or **might not** for actions or things that will possibly not happen.

-   *She looks very tired. She **might not come** with us.*
-   *We **may not have** enough time to finish the report for tomorrow.*
